paras: The lynching of George Kincaid was the killing of a Black man whose body was found hanging in a swamp near Cleveland, Mississippi, in late June 1903, days after a mob gathered at Ruleville to lynch him. Kincaid was accused of having seriously wounded two white men, John Brock and George Stoakley, five years earlier. Wire reports said a deputy sheriff had surrendered him on a written order to a man named Jackson, and the New York Sun reported that no one knew who killed him. Papers in the North headlined the five-year gap between the alleged shooting and the hanging, and the case was carried in the year's lynching lists.

According to a Cleveland special to the New Orleans Picayune, Kincaid was the man who had "seriously wounded" John Brock and George Stoakely five years before. Other reports gave the charge differently: the Sun said he "shot John Breck and George Stoakely" and called him a negro "Who Murdered Two Men," while the Indianapolis Freeman wrote that he was hanged "for murder committed five years ago."

On Saturday a mob gathered at Ruleville to lynch Kincaid. The Sun's account said he was arrested in Ruleville that day and, after threats of lynching, was taken to Cleveland "for safety." In the Picayune's version, Deputy Sheriff Riddle "spirited" him to Cleveland, where Deputy Sheriff McGuire agreed to hold him only after Riddle promised to come back and stay with him.

Riddle did not return; instead an order signed by him arrived directing that the prisoner be delivered to the bearer, a man named Jackson, and this was done. A shorter version of the wire said the order was signed by "another deputy sheriff," while the Wichita Daily Eagle's text had Riddle himself giving Kincaid into Jackson's keeping. Kincaid's body was then found hanging from the branch of a tree in a swamp near Cleveland.

A New Orleans dispatch to the Sun on June 25 said there was "some mystery" about the killing and "a disposition to shoulder the blame on the officers of Bolivar county," and that it was not known who killed him. It also reported that, "in consequence of the trouble at Ruleville," about 200 armed Black men threatened the whites and then dispersed when a large force of whites arrived. No report of an inquest, an arrest or a prosecution appears in the coverage.

White papers carried the story on June 24 and 25, mostly as the Picayune special or a shortened wire version, and only the Sun's later dispatch pointed toward the county officers. It ran on the front pages of the Savannah Morning News, the Birmingham Age-Herald and other dailies. Headlines stressed the swamp and the delay: "Hanged in a Swamp" in Montgomery, "Lynched After Five Years" in the New-York Tribune, whose deck read "Mississippians Show Long Memory for Negro Criminal." The Wichita Daily Eagle stated the charge as fact in its deck, "This Negro Committed a Crime Two Years Ago," with a different interval from its own text.
Condensed digest items in the Minneapolis Journal and in North Dakota weeklies dropped the deputies and the order and said instead that Kincaid had been "taken from the authorities by a mob."

In the Black press, the Wisconsin Weekly Advocate ran a one-sentence item headed "Lynching Near Cleveland" in a column of mob news, under a misprinted "Cleveland, O." dateline. The Indianapolis Freeman's editorial paragraphs placed the case in a "carnival of mobs" in which "the colored man is the center of attraction," and remarked that "they have very good memories in Mississippi." Monthly lynching lists in the Freeman, the Seattle Republican and several white papers entered him under June 23 at Cleveland, Miss., and the Pine Bluff Daily Graphic gave his offense as "murderous assault."

The date is uncertain: the Picayune's dispatch of June 23 said the body was found that day, and the lynching lists used June 23, but the Wisconsin Weekly Advocate's item of June 24 said Kincaid was lynched "early this morning" and the Sun's dispatch of June 25 said "yesterday." The June 23 dispatch is the earliest and comes from Cleveland, so it is the stronger evidence.

The Sun connected the armed gathering of about 200 Black men to the Ruleville trouble, but a Ruleville dispatch of June 23 in the Weekly Corinthian described a gathering of about 200 at Pentecost caused by "the killing of a negro by a plantation manager last Friday," without mentioning Kincaid.

reader.title: Lynching of George Kincaid
bases: A Black man accused of an old shooting was handed out of a deputy's custody on a signed order and found hanged in a swamp after a mob had gathered to lynch him [A2][A13].

Kincaid was hanged without legal process after removal from custody, under an accusation of wounding two men [A2][A13]; a mob gathered to lynch him and digests say a mob took him [A1][A9], but the fullest account names only Jackson as taking him and the Sun says the killers are unknown [A2][A13].

The Picayune's Cleveland special and the Sun's separate New Orleans dispatch agree that a Ruleville mob sought him and he was found hanging in a swamp near Cleveland [A2][A13], and independent lynching lists record it [A20][A19].

accounts.label: Picayune's Cleveland special
accounts.gist: Riddle spirited Kincaid away from a Ruleville mob to Cleveland; McGuire reluctantly held him; an order signed by Riddle delivered him to Jackson, and the body was found hanging in the swamps.

accounts.label: Short wire version
accounts.gist: Same story with the order signed by 'another deputy sheriff'; the Black-press brief reduces it to a lynching near Ruleville of a Negro who wounded two white men.

accounts.label: Sun's New Orleans dispatch
accounts.gist: Kincaid was arrested in Ruleville and taken to Cleveland for safety; the lynching was a 'mystery' with blame directed at Bolivar county officers; 200 armed Black men threatened whites and dispersed.

accounts.label: News digests
accounts.gist: Kincaid was taken from the authorities by a mob and hanged.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Picayune special or short wire under headlines like 'Hanged in a Swamp' and 'Found a Negro's Body Hanging From a Tree', presenting the accusation as fact.
The New-York Tribune headlined 'Lynched After Five Years. Mississippians Show Long Memory for Negro Criminal'; the Sun noted 'some mystery' and suspicion of county officers.
The Wisconsin Weekly Advocate printed a one-sentence wire item 'Lynching Near Cleveland' amid other mob news.
The Indianapolis Freeman listed it in a 'carnival of mobs' in which 'the colored man is the center of attraction', with irony about Mississippi's 'very good memories'.

Hanging, killing and removal from custody are supported; no shooting of Kincaid or siege is reported (the shooting is the five-year-old accusation).

info: Body found hanging in a swamp near Cleveland, reported found 'today' in a dispatch dated June 23, 1903; mob had gathered at Ruleville the previous Saturday (June 20). Other versions: lynched early June 24 (Advocate), 'yesterday' June 24 (Sun); lists give June 23.
Mob gathered at Ruleville; prisoner taken to Cleveland; body found in a swamp near Cleveland, Miss. Variants: 'Puleville', 'Rushville', 'Cleveland, O.'

Accused of having seriously wounded John Brock and George Stoakley/Stoakely five years earlier; the Sun says he shot 'John Breck' and George Stoakely and heads him as having 'Murdered Two Men'; the Freeman says 'murder'; the Advocate and Willmar Tribune say the two were white men.
Unknown; the Sun says 'It is not known who killed the negro'; a man named Jackson took custody on a deputy's signed order; condensed reports say a mob.
